item.title: Explaining Guernica to Mozart
item.dc:creator: Chamber Music Society
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to The Art of Listening! In this installment, author Jan Swafford describes an imaginary conversation in which he attempts to explain Pablo Picasso’s painting Guernica (1937) to Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.

Picasso (1881–1973) and Mozart (1756–91) lived during very different times and had very different conceptions of art. For Mozart, art involved rules and codes; how an artist operated within those rules and codes defined the artist. But for Picasso, art was an expression of emotions, ideas, and messages; rules and codes were put aside, and how the viewer experienced the work was everything.

It’s difficult for many listeners, even today, to wrap their heads around modernism in classical music. But in this newsletter, Swafford uses a dialogue with Mozart about Guernica to show how the artistic thinking of the 20th century evolved from—and has a place in—the 18th. Be sure to check out our playlist: a juxtaposition of chamber music by Mozart and 20th-century composers.

Subscribe now

Recently in Madrid I stood for a while in front of Pablo Picasso’s painting Guernica, thinking about how to explain it to Mozart.

I often speak to my biographical subjects while I’m writing about them. A while back I spent some time playing Louis Armstrong for Johannes Brahms. I felt sure he would catch on and like it. After all, he was fascinated the time he heard an American girl playing ragtime on banjo.

Talking to Mozart about Guernica was dicier business. I wasn’t sure he could ever get his sensibility around it. There are so many issues at play in that soul-searing painting, done soon after the atrocity that inspired it: the fire-bombing of a Basque village by Nazi warplanes in support of General Francisco Franco. He ordained, in other words, the mass murder of his own people, most of them women and children.

I’d begin by showing Mozart a photograph. I’d tell him that when photography appeared, painting was no longer required to represent reality. Now painting could take off on its own, free of representation. Art could distort reality at will, or depart from it entirely and treat painting as an abstraction—like instrumental music.

Already I might have lost Mozart. He was so tied to his time, to convention. He made use of conventions—musical, dramatic, operatic—to the end of his life, wielding them as part of his singular voice. Mozart might never be prepared to understand modernism in art; he was interested in using the status quo for his own purposes.

But let’s imagine that, in the middle of me explaining art of the early 20th century to Mozart, he hadn’t run off screaming—that he remained, skeptical but ready to hear more. I’d show him Picasso’s cubism, how it distorted reality while remaining true to it, and how those distortions could be expressive and human, even as the works bent and folded matter like a sheet of paper. I’d show him Picasso’s cubist paintings of a woman crying and point out that you can still see her pain.

Then I’d show Mozart airplanes, particularly warplanes dropping bombs. He would be shocked and stunned. He would see an evil he could scarcely comprehend. His view of war involved glory and heroism and grand uniforms. Planes dropping bombs have no glory, no heroism; their purpose is slaughter. I can’t imagine that Mozart’s kind of art could encompass that kind of evil.

Then I would tell him about the bombing of Guernica by German airplanes, sanctioned by Franco. Finally, I would show him Picasso’s painting. It would need to be in person, standing in front of that massive, horrifying canvas.

I think on some level Mozart would understand. How could he not? It is a painting whose essential point is inescapable. I’d explain to him that in this painting the distortions of cubism are put at the service of portraying unspeakable violence and pain, a world broken and weeping and screaming—woman screams, nature screams, virile bull screams. On the ground lies a shattered statue, one disjointed hand clutching a broken sword: art is broken too, and the statue is screaming.

All very well, Mozart would say, but this painting is like the daubing of a little child! I would respond by showing him the work of Picasso in his teens, when he could already draw traditional representations remarkably well. I’d explain that his skill at drawing stayed with him, but he came to feel that he had to tear it up, put it aside, and draw, with all his skill, as if he were a child. This would be another point at which Mozart might throw up his hands. The idea that you would use your skill to mask your skill! To Mozart, skill meant a great deal. My only response would be that if Guernica were painted any other way, it wouldn’t have the same kind of power.

Art has changed fundamentally since Mozart’s day, and those changes have dragged his art along with them. The connection of art to the world has changed, everything from “art for art’s sake” to bloody involvement in the horrors of the day.

Still, musical responses to war are not new. Joseph Haydn’s Mass in Time of War (1796), and Ludwig van Beethoven’s Missa solemnis (1819–23) are both shattered during the prayer for peace in the “Agnus Dei” by sounds of war that tear the music apart—as the statue in Guernica is blown apart. But Picasso, within the language of cubism, has reached a depiction of pain and tragedy rawer, more immediate, than almost anything before.

I suppose what I believe is that a response to suffering or evil that boils up from inside an artist is an authentic work: artists responding to the world. All the same, to make a protest meaningful you still have to paint, or compose, well. Picasso’s response to evil is immortal because it’s a great painting by a great artist—not because of its protest, which is intentionally so simple a child can understand it.

Picasso labored at white heat for a month on Guernica, revising it again and again, because he insisted it must work not just as statement, but as art. Surely that’s why Guernica is one of the mightiest works of its kind.

This reminds me of the revisions Henry David Thoreau made to a line in his 1854 book Walden. It began with an observation at a party, something like, “I noticed that most of the people there put on a convivial face, but it was clear that none of them were really happy in the least, yet they never talk about it.” Then he began working on the idea—as I remember there are nine surviving drafts of it. What he ended up with is one of the most famous phrases in the English language: “The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.” That phrase doesn’t say anything the first version didn’t, but it says it once and for all: we spend our lives learning its truth.

Let’s remember what Picasso said: “Art is a lie that makes us realize truth.” I think Mozart would understand that completely.

Further Reading

  • “Pablo Picasso” – Francesca Ferrari

    • A brief introduction to Picasso from the Museum of Modern Art.

  • Mozart: The Reign of Love (2020) – Jan Swafford

    • An engaging, highly readable biography of Mozart by the author of this week’s newsletter.

  • Mozart: A Life (1995) – Maynard Solomon

    • Written by the famed musicologist (and co-founder of Vanguard Records) Maynard Solomon, this engrossing, approachable book is often described as the definitive biography of Mozart.

  • Mozart’s Letters, Mozart’s Life (2000) – ed./trans. Robert Spaethling

    • A collection of Mozart’s letters, preserving the eccentricities, misspellings, and bawdy humor that formed the lifeblood of his personality.

  • Mozart in Motion: His Work and His World in Pieces (2021) – Patrick Mackie

    • A journey through Mozart’s life, viewed through the lens of his compositions.

item.title: A Dream and a Passion: Mendelssohn’s Revival of a Bach Masterpiece
item.dc:creator: Chamber Music Society
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to The Art of Listening! In this installment, we discuss how vital the Romantic composer Felix Mendelssohn (1809–1847) was to our current perspective of the Baroque composer Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750). Given Bach’s towering figure today, it is tempting to believe that he was always viewed this way. But the truth is that after his death, only a small number of people outside Leipzig—primarily connoisseurs—were familiar with Bach’s works. He was remembered as a keyboard virtuoso, but the music that was known was mainly for keyboard and educational purposes. It is in large part because of the 19th-century “Bach revival” that his name is so well known today. And at the forefront of that movement was Mendelssohn, who led an 1829 performance of Bach’s St. Matthew Passion, an oratorio that had fallen into relative obscurity.

In this newsletter, writer and critic Paul Griffiths tells the story of how Mendelssohn resurrected the music and the image of Bach through his role as a conductor and a Bach enthusiast. Be sure to check out Bach’s St. Matthew Passion below.

Subscribe now

One of the most significant concerts in music history took place on Wednesday, March 11, 1829, at the Singakademie in Berlin: the first performance of J.S. Bach’s St. Matthew Passion (1727) in almost a century. In the audience were the poet Heinrich Heine, the philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, and the King of Prussia, Frederick William III. The German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (who was not there but was given a report of the event) wrote about the performance: “To me it is as if I was hearing from afar the roaring of the sea.”

The one responsible for that roar—the one conducting and playing piano to accompany the Gospel narratives—was a young man of 20: Felix Mendelssohn. He had been leading weekly rehearsals of the work for over a year (and had been studying it for five), but his enthusiasm for Bach, inherited from his maternal grandmother, Bella Salomon, and her sister Sara Levy, went back further.

The children of a Jewish banker, these sisters were brought up in a cultured environment where the music of Bach was highly esteemed. One of Bach’s foremost pupils was brought in to teach the young Bella; Sara kept up lessons for a decade with Bach’s eldest son, Wilhelm Friedemann Bach. Both sisters married within the comfortable Jewish milieu of Berlin, and both remained active collectors and promoters of Bach’s music. Both made sure their passion was transmitted to Felix Mendelssohn and his sister Fanny—a pianist and composer herself.

Bella commissioned a copy of the score of the St. Matthew Passion to give to her grandson on his 15th birthday, but died before his 1829 performance. Sara, living in Berlin, could have been there, though the subject matter might have kept her away: both sisters held to the Jewish faith of their ancestors and were dismayed when younger members of the family, including Mendelssohn’s parents, converted to Christianity.

Mendelssohn was baptized at the age of seven by a Protestant pastor, but he was also proud of his Jewish ancestry. We don’t know whether he was a regular churchgoer, but he probably wasn’t; he was most likely a firm adherent of the Church of Johann Sebastian Bach, in company with many musicians and music lovers. Following Bach, he set texts from the Hebrew Bible in the solid, affirmative voice of Martin Luther’s German, as in his several psalm settings. But his strongest sacred piece, Mitten wir im Leben sind (In the midst of life)—a work based on one of Luther’s chorales and composed the year after the St. Matthew Passion performance—contains little that is explicitly Christian.

Mendelssohn also displayed his continuing reverence for Bach in the sets of preludes and fugues he wrote for piano and organ. (The genre of preludes-and-fugues was popularized by Bach’s keyboard work The Well-Tempered Clavier.) Besides all this, he gave a series of concerts at the St. Thomas Church in Leipzig (Bach’s church) to raise money for a Bach monument there: an organ recital in 1840, a performance of the St. Matthew Passion the following year, and then a program of Bach pieces on the day of the monument’s unveiling in 1843. Since the proceeds failed to cover the monument’s cost, he supplemented them out of his own pocket.

As a result of Mendelssohn’s activities, more of Bach’s music began to appear in print, beginning with the St. Matthew Passion in 1830. Mendelssohn also made a significant contribution to the development of a musical culture based not only on new works, but also on a “standard repertoire”—an established body of classic works. What was new then is now familiar to us. But classical music today is still largely concerned with reviving and rehearing great works, and, because of Mendelssohn, we can now experience the St. Matthew Passion in innumerable different forms—including the version, cut and rescored, that he presented almost two centuries ago.
